messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 65
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Special Education Teacher
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 35

He is a 65-year-old Latin American man who comes across as measured and self-contained, the kind of person who has spent much of his life managing difficult feelings by keeping them in order. He is divorced and lives alone now, though he remains deeply identified with his work as a special education teacher, a role that seems to fit the part of him that has always wanted to protect, organize, and make sense of what feels chaotic. Over several sessions, he describes a life shaped by military service, and the events that stay with him are not remembered as a single dramatic moment so much as a long stretch of fear, vigilance, and moral confusion that began in young adulthood and never quite ended.

He first goes into the military believing, like many young men of his generation, that service will give him direction and dignity. He speaks of the early months with a mix of pride and unease. There is structure, camaraderie, and the sense that his body and mind must always be ready. The traumatic period comes later, during deployment, when the world becomes defined by waiting, alarms, and sudden violence. He does not describe one event in a theatrical way; instead, he remembers a series of scenes that blend together: the blast of artillery, the sound of men shouting, the smell of dust and metal, the sight of someone who had been standing beside him and is not standing there anymore. He recalls learning, almost immediately, that survival depends on staying alert even when exhausted, even when terrified. He says he stopped sleeping well there, not because he was weak, but because sleeping felt like letting go of the only control he had.

After returning home, he expects to settle back into civilian life, but he finds that his body continues to behave as though danger is nearby. He startles at sudden noises, especially anything sharp and metallic. Fireworks, car backfires, even the slam of a heavy classroom door can make his shoulders jump and his heart race before he can explain to himself what happened. He notices himself scanning rooms automatically, locating exits, watching people’s hands, sitting with his back to the wall when he can. He dislikes feeling trapped, and if he is in a crowded place, he becomes tense and irritable, eager to leave before he can admit why. He has developed a habit of choosing seats strategically and checking locks more than once, behaviors he does not advertise to others because he worries they would seem excessive.

For years he tries to outrun the memories by working hard. Teaching becomes both refuge and structure. He is good with students who need patience and consistency, and he takes pride in being the adult who stays calm when a child is melting down. Yet the work also stirs things in him. He is especially alert to loud voices, sudden movements, and the look of panic on a child’s face. He can remain steady on the outside, but inside he feels the old tension rise. At times a smell, a sound, or the particular dry heat of a classroom in late afternoon brings him back to a place he does not want to revisit. He does not fully lose contact with the present, but he becomes distant, his mind pulled toward images he would rather not name. He speaks of “going somewhere else” for a moment, then having to catch up again to what people are saying.

He has also become more distant from others over time. His marriage did not survive the years in which he remained emotionally guarded and difficult to soothe. He describes himself as loving his family but being unable to fully let them in, especially when the memories grew stronger. His wife eventually experienced him as unavailable, preoccupied, and sometimes angry without warning. He does not frame the divorce as anyone’s fault, but there is a quiet grief in how he tells it. Now he is more isolated than he once imagined he would be, though he maintains contact with a few colleagues and adult relatives. He tries to be social but finds it draining, and he often prefers the company of routine over that of people.

At night, he still sleeps lightly. He wakes from dreams that leave him disoriented and damp with sweat, though he does not always remember the content. Sometimes he senses danger before he can identify it, and for a few moments his body reacts as if he is back in the field. On those mornings he gets up early, makes coffee, and sits with the television on low volume, using noise to interrupt the quiet. He has learned to keep moving, to keep teaching, to keep showing up. Even now, at 65, he carries the war in the background of daily life, not constantly visible but never fully absent, woven into the way he watches the world, measures risk, and tries to stay prepared for what might happen next.
